title: How donyou get AI to test the things it adds?
author: Kalicola
selftext:
I’ve been experimenting with a brick breaker game using ai.. the controls are simple, move left and right, that’s it..

The ai says it’s testing the game, but it never moves the pad around, nothing happens.. It even said that it can’t move the pad, because it’s tapping the controls so fast that it doesn’t move..

Is there a trick to get the ai to actually play and test the game?  
I’m using chatgpt codex

comments.author: Jarfino
comments.body: Try telling it to make a driver that uses the same inputs a human would for running your tests

comments.author: legend-of-alan
comments.body:
Have a separate agent Write the tests first. Then have the ai write the code without looking at the tests.

Tests should not pin implementation, just externally visible behavior.

Look into behavior driven design (BDD). This has become very popular since ai became big for exactly the reason your describing.

Using a feature map can help the ai use your interface and controls properly outside of code.

Hope this helps!

replies.author: Kalicola
replies.body:
I did not understand any of that 😆  
Perhaps I’m ready yet

comments.author: Mrbuttshaman
comments.body: I have it use another agent that runs into walls to test collision in a window-less session.  That was enough to fix all my collision problems that I had.

comments.author: Abject-Constant784
comments.body:
Step 1: switch to Claude. 

Jokes aside, I've never used GPT, I've only used claude, but it builds full test cases, scripts, and Claude then builds and runs VMs to play the games I have it building. I have it running GODOT 4.7 in a VM as well, so I don't even have to have it using a MCP server on my PC. It just uses the VM. 

Maybe try prompting your GPT with something to trigger VM functions, test cases, audit proofs, etc. and if that doesn't work... See step 1. Lol

replies.author: Abject-Constant784
replies.body:
Nah just take some time to research it! 

VM is a virtual machine. Some AIs have the capability to run them on their hardware to run tests. Test cases are just pre determined actions or requirements you want fulfilled for a specific outcome. And if that outcome isn't reached, then it goes back and tries again. Etc.

There's several very in depth courses on AI and how to get started. I think Google actually has one that's free through Coursera that gives you 3 months of Google Gemini pro subscription, haven't looked into it much, but worth checking out.

replies.author: Abject-Constant784
replies.body: If it makes you feel any better, I started off pretty new. I have some background in Java from my highschool days and a year in uni, but that was like 13+ years ago. I barely remember any of that. So to do what I want with AI I had to learn proper design, coding methodology, AI prompting safe practices etc. over the past year or so. With a proper course or learning plan that you develop you can learn it in a month or two easily if you have the time and motivation. Best of luck! 👍

comments.author: JakSilver00
comments.body:
I see that you're commenting about the language barrier and you may need to elaborate on that more but you simply tell the agent that you need to build a test harness that should act as an automated CPU-driven player initially you'll want to start out and say what it should be doing at some point you'll want to keep logs of these things and then tell it for each new function we add have something that can test that.  
  
There are at least six different ways to do this. I think the most linear way is when you're building the game, build it as if there wasn't going to be a human player. That way you're basically trying to build a video of gameplay, and then you just say this is what it should do, and then have some kind of toggle to switch from automated to manual controls.

Additionally, Claude and GPT for some reason act wildly different. One is better at gameplay and filling in gaps while the other is better at following instructions and technical aspects. And yes, I recommend using both if you can actually take time to build a small interface or looping system that incorporates both of them into your projects and then delegates tasks accordingly, it makes everything way easier. Additionally, it depends on if you have an MCP, a CLI, or you're just modifying the back-end data.

replies.author: JakSilver00
replies.body: If you decide to reply to this, please confirm that you're still working on the rat game or describe what you're actually trying to do that way I can provide a more detailed explanation specific to your game.
